messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Karim

Karim was twenty-two when it happened, a Friday night in March at an apartment near campus where he had gone with someone he thought he trusted. He had known this person casually for weeks—they shared a mutual friend, had texted back and forth, and the invitation to hang out had felt ordinary, safe. The apartment was dark and smelled of stale cigarette smoke and something chemical underneath, a scent Karim could not quite place. When he tried to leave the bedroom later that night, his refusals had been ignored. The physical violation itself had lasted perhaps ten minutes, though time had become unreliable in his memory—sometimes it felt like seconds, sometimes like hours. What remained sharp was the smell, that acrid chemical undercurrent mixed with cologne and sweat, a sensory signature his brain had burned into a warning system.

In the weeks following, Karim had said nothing to anyone. He had gone back to his apartment, showered, and tried to pretend the evening had not occurred. But his body had other ideas. By the time he returned to his job as an auditor at a mid-sized firm in downtown Chicago, something fundamental had shifted. His role required him to visit client sites across the city and suburbs, to evaluate their financial records and procedures, which meant navigating unfamiliar office buildings, conference rooms, and parking structures. Within two weeks of the assault, Karim found himself unable to enter a building he had not visited before. The uncertainty was unbearable—he could not assess what might happen, where the exits were, who might be present. He began making excuses to his supervisor, claiming scheduling conflicts, then illness. His manager had started to notice the pattern.

What had once been manageable—sitting in a client's conference room, presenting audit findings—had become a minefield of threat. Whenever someone shifted suddenly in their chair or leaned forward across the table, Karim's entire nervous system would spike into readiness, his shoulders tensing, his breath catching. He had come to believe that others could see something in him, something marked or damaged, and this fear had crystallized into a strategy: he wore dark, oversized sweaters and button-up shirts that concealed his frame, kept his hair longer to shadow his face, anything to avoid being noticed, evaluated, or singled out. In meetings, he positioned himself always near the door, his leg jiggling beneath the table, his attention divided between the audit materials and the geometry of escape routes.

The smell that had trapped itself in his memory had become omnipresent. A colleague's cologne triggered a cascade of panic. The cleaning solution used in the office bathroom sent him into the stairwell. He had begun to notice that certain scents appeared without warning—a stranger's perfume on the street, a restaurant kitchen exhaust—and each time, his body would flood with the same dread.

What haunted him most was a quieter, more insidious thought: someone else would never have gone to that apartment. Someone else would have seen the danger earlier, would have trusted their instincts, would not have put themselves in that position. He had internalized a permanent sense of failure, as if the assault had exposed a fundamental weakness in his judgment. He remembered being happy before, genuinely happy—he had laughed easily, had gone out with friends without calculation, had felt at home in his own skin. Now he was always braced, always miserable, always aware of the distance between who he had been and who he had become. The humiliation was not something that would fade; it was a permanent stain on how he understood himself.

By late autumn, Karim's manager had scheduled a meeting to discuss his performance. The conversation had been gentle, but the message was clear: something had to change. It was this conversation, more than the assault itself, that finally pushed him to seek help. He was terrified of losing his job, terrified of being exposed as someone damaged, but more than that, he was exhausted by the constant vigilance, the endless calculations of safety, the person he had become. When he called the clinic, his voice was steady, but his hands were shaking. He wanted to know if it was possible to feel safe again, or if he would always be this way.
